holdings.statement: Second, transferee may refrain from withdrawing funds to ensure sufficient care for ageing parent, despite legal and beneficial entitlement.

holdings.quote: 66 Finally, as previously discussed, the fact that a transferor controlled and used the funds during his or her life is not necessarily inconsistent with an intention at the time of the transfer that the transferee would acquire the balance of the account on the transferor’s death through the gift of the right of survivorship.
holdings.statement: Third, transferor's control and use of funds during life is not inconsistent with intent that transferee acquire balance on death via right of survivorship.

holdings.quote: 68 I share Lang J.A.’s view that the trier of fact has the discretion to consider the granting of power of attorney when deciding the transferor’s intention.
holdings.statement: The trier of fact has discretion to consider granting of power of attorney when deciding transferor's intention.

holdings.quote: This will be especially true when other evidence suggests that the transferor appreciated the distinction between granting that power and gifting the right of survivorship.
holdings.statement: Consideration of power of attorney is especially relevant when other evidence shows transferor understood difference between power of attorney and gifting right of survivorship.

holdings.quote: Again however, this evidence will not be determinative and courts should use caution in relying upon it, because it is entirely plausible that the transferor granted power of attorney and placed his or her assets in a joint account but nevertheless intended that the balance of the account be distributed according to his or her will.
holdings.statement: Evidence of granting power of attorney is not determinative; transferor may grant power of attorney and joint account for convenience but intend distribution by will.

holdings.quote: For example, the transferor may have granted power of attorney in order to have assistance with other affairs beyond the account and may have made the transferee a joint account holder solely for added convenience.
holdings.statement: Transferor may grant power of attorney for assistance beyond the account and make transferee joint account holder solely for convenience.

holdings.quote: I do not find either of these approaches inappropriate.
holdings.statement: I do not find either of these approaches inappropriate.

holdings.quote: The weight to be placed on tax-related evidence in determining a transferor’s intent should be left to the discretion of the trial judge.
holdings.statement: The weight to be placed on tax-related evidence in determining a transferor’s intent should be left to the discretion of the trial judge.

holdings.quote: However, whether or not a transferor continues to pay taxes on the income earned in the joint accounts during his or her lifetime should not be determinative of his or her intention in the absence of other evidence.
holdings.statement: Whether or not a transferor continues to pay taxes on the income earned in the joint accounts during his or her lifetime should not be determinative of his or her intention in the absence of other evidence.

holdings.quote: For example, it may be that the transferor made the transfer for the sole purpose of obtaining assistance in the management of his or her finances and wished to have the assets form a part of his or her estate upon his or her death.
holdings.statement: It may be that the transferor made the transfer for the sole purpose of obtaining assistance in the management of his or her finances and wished to have the assets form a part of his or her estate upon his or her death.

holdings.quote: Or, as discussed above, it is open to a transferor to gift the right of survivorship to the transferee when the joint accounts are opened, but to retain control over the use of the funds in the accounts (and therefore to continue to pay taxes on them) during his or her lifetime.
holdings.statement: It is open to a transferor to gift the right of survivorship to the transferee when the joint accounts are opened, but to retain control over the use of the funds in the accounts (and therefore to continue to pay taxes on them) during his or her lifetime.

holdings.quote: In principle, I agree.
holdings.statement: In principle, the Court agrees that transferors should not be allowed to transfer beneficial title while avoiding capital gains taxes.

holdings.quote: Where, in setting up a joint account, the transferor intends to transfer full legal and equitable title to the assets in the account immediately and the value of the assets reflects a capital gain, taxes on capital gains may become payable in the year the joint account is set up.
holdings.statement: Where the transferor intends to transfer full legal and equitable title immediately in setting up a joint account, capital gains taxes may become payable in that year.

holdings.quote: However, where the transferor’s intention is to gift the right of survivorship to the transferee but retain beneficial ownership of the assets during his or her lifetime, there would appear to be no disposition at the moment of the setting up of the joint account: see s. 73 of the Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp .).
holdings.statement: Where the transferor intends to gift only the right of survivorship but retain beneficial ownership during lifetime, there is no disposition at the time of setting up the joint account for tax purposes.

holdings.quote: That said, the issue of the proper treatment of capital gains in the setting up of joint accounts was not argued in this appeal.
holdings.statement: The issue of proper tax treatment of capital gains in joint accounts was not argued in this appeal.

holdings.quote: I agree with the trial judge that “if [the father’s] intention was to have his jointly held assets devolve through the estate, they were of such magnitude that he would have at least discussed that matter with his solicitor, since they constituted a substantial proportion of what he owned” (para. 43), particularly after the lawyer asked him about life insurance policies, RRIFs and other assets.
holdings.statement: The Court agrees that if the father intended the jointly held assets to devolve through the estate, he would have discussed it with his solicitor given their substantial value.

holdings.quote: All of this evidence is consistent with Paula’s father having gifted away the right of survivorship when the joint accounts were opened, and thus is relevant to his intention at the time of the transfer.
holdings.statement: All evidence is consistent with the father having gifted the right of survivorship when the joint accounts were opened, relevant to his intention at transfer.

holdings.quote: I agree with the trial judge that this is not inconsistent with an intention that the balance remaining in the accounts would belong to Paula on his death.
holdings.statement: The Court agrees this intention to avoid immediate tax is not inconsistent with the intention that the balance would belong to Paula on death.

holdings.quote: Karam J. should therefore have applied the presumption of a resulting trust.
holdings.statement: The presumption of resulting trust should have been applied instead of the presumption of advancement.

holdings.quote: Nonetheless, this error does not affect the ultimate disposition of the appeal because the trial judge found that the evidence “clearly demonstrate[d] the intention” on the part of the father that the balance left in the joint accounts he had with Paula were to go to Paula alone on his death through survivorship (para. 44).
holdings.statement: Despite the error, the trial judge found clear evidence of the father’s intention that the balance in the joint accounts go to Paula on his death.

holdings.quote: I am satisfied that this strong finding regarding the father’s actual intention shows that the trial judge’s conclusion would have been the same even if he had applied the presumption of a resulting trust.
holdings.statement: The Court is satisfied the trial judge’s conclusion would be the same even if the presumption of resulting trust had been applied.

holdings.quote: 76 For the reasons above, I would dismiss this appeal, with costs.
holdings.statement: The appeal is dismissed with costs.

holdings.quote: I see no reason to interfere with that disposition, or that costs should not follow the event in this Court.
holdings.statement: There is no reason to interfere with the trial judge's disposition on costs, but costs should follow the event in this Court.

holdings.quote: 78 This appeal involves a father who opened joint bank accounts with his daughter, signing documents that specifically confirmed that the daughter was to have a survivorship interest. The daughter’s entitlement to the remaining funds in the accounts was challenged by her ex-husband.
holdings.statement: The appeal involves a father who opened joint bank accounts with his daughter, confirming her survivorship interest, and the daughter's entitlement was challenged by her ex-husband.

holdings.quote: 79 Historically, the presumption of advancement has been applied to gratuitous transfers to children, regardless of the child’s age. If we are to continue to retain the presumption of advancement for parent-child transfers, I see no reason, unlike Rothstein J., to limit its application to non-adult children.
holdings.statement: The presumption of advancement has historically applied to gratuitous transfers to children regardless of age, and its application should not be limited to non-adult children.

holdings.quote: I agree with him, however, that the scope of the presumption should be expanded to include transfers from mothers as well as from fathers.
holdings.statement: The presumption of advancement should be expanded to include transfers from mothers as well as fathers.

holdings.quote: 80 The presumptions of advancement and resulting trust are legal tools which assist in determining the transferor’s intention at the time a gratuitous transfer is made. The tools are of particular significance when the transferor has died.
holdings.statement: The presumptions of advancement and resulting trust are legal tools to assist in determining the transferor's intention at the time of a gratuitous transfer, especially when the transferor has died.

holdings.quote: 81 If the presumption of advancement applies, an individual who transfers property into another person’s name is presumed to have intended to make a gift to that person. The burden of proving that the transfer was not intended to be a gift, is on the challenger to the transfer. If the presumption of resulting trust applies, the transferor is presumed to have intended to retain the beneficial ownership. The burden of proving that a gift was intended, is on the recipient of the transfer.
holdings.statement: If the presumption of advancement applies, the transferor is presumed to have intended a gift, and the challenger bears the burden of proving no gift was intended; if the presumption of resulting trust applies, the transferor is presumed to retain beneficial ownership, and the recipient bears the burden of proving a gift was intended.

holdings.quote: 84 McHugh J.’s allusion to “earlier centuries” reflects the origins of the presumption of resulting trust. In the 15th century, it was not uncommon for landowners in England to have title to their property held by other individuals on the understanding that it was being held for the “use” of the landowner and subject to his direction. This had the effect of separating legal and beneficial ownership. The purpose of the scheme was to avoid having to pay feudal taxes when land passed from a landowner to his heir.
holdings.statement: The presumption of resulting trust originated in 15th century England where landowners had legal title held by others for their use to avoid feudal taxes, separating legal and beneficial ownership.

holdings.quote: 85 It became so common for owners to transfer land to be held for their own use, that the courts began to presume that a transfer made without consideration, or gratuitously, was intended to be for the transferor’s own use, giving rise to the presumption of resulting use. Because these nominal transfers caused a significant loss of revenue to the Crown, the Statute of Uses, 1535 was enacted, which “executed the use”, reuniting legal and equitable title (R. Chambers, “Resulting Trusts in Canada” (2000), 38 Alta. L. Rev. 378; Cho Ki Yau Trust (Trustees of) v. Yau Estate (1999), 29 E.T.R. (2d) 204 (Ont. S.C.J.)).
holdings.statement: Because such nominal transfers caused revenue loss, the Statute of Uses 1535 was enacted to reunite legal and equitable title, leading to the presumption of resulting trust as a vestigial doctrine.

holdings.quote: 86 The presumption of resulting trust is the vestigial doctrine that emerged from the evolutionary remains of the executed use. The presumption of advancement, on the other hand, evolved as a limited exception to the presumption of resulting trust, generally arising in two situations: when a gratuitous transfer was made by a father to his child; and when a gratuitous transfer was made by a husband to his wife.
holdings.statement: The presumption of resulting trust is a vestigial doctrine from the executed use, while the presumption of advancement evolved as a limited exception, generally applying to gratuitous transfers from father to child or husband to wife.

holdings.quote: Parental affection, no less than parental obligation, has always grounded the presumption of advancement.
holdings.statement: Parental affection, no less than parental obligation, has always grounded the presumption of advancement.

holdings.quote: 96 But in most cases, the presumption of advancement continues to be applied to gratuitous transfers from parents to their children, regardless of age. In Madsen Estate v. Saylor, for example, the companion appeal, the Ontario Court of Appeal found that the trial judge erred in applying the presumption of resulting trust, concluding that “the presumption of advancement can still apply to transfers of property from a father to a child, including an independent adult child” ((2005), 261 D.L.R. (4th) 597, at para. 21).
holdings.statement: In most cases, the presumption of advancement continues to be applied to gratuitous transfers from parents to their children, regardless of age.

holdings.quote: 106 Equally, a presumed intention of joint ownership in the case of jointly held property should apply to parent-child relationships, and the appropriate mechanism for achieving this objective, absent legislative intervention, is the application of the presumption of advancement.
holdings.statement: The presumption of advancement should apply to presumed joint ownership in parent-child relationships absent legislative intervention.

holdings.quote: 107 The trial judge, whose conclusion was upheld by the Court of Appeal, properly applied the correct legal presumption to the facts of the case.
holdings.statement: The trial judge properly applied the correct legal presumption to the facts of the case, and this conclusion was upheld by the Court of Appeal.

holdings.quote: Like Rothstein J., therefore, I would dismiss the appeal.
holdings.statement: The appeal is dismissed.

holdings.quote: Appeal dismissed with costs.
holdings.statement: Appeal dismissed with costs.

authorities.quote: The beneficial owner of property has been described as “the real owner of property even though it is in someone else’s name”: Csak v. Aumon (1990), 69 D.L.R. (4th) 567 (Ont. H.C.J.), at p. 570.
authorities.authority: Beneficial ownership is described as the real ownership of property even if in another's name, as in Csak v. Aumon (1990).

authorities.quote: Re Mailman Estate, [1941] S.C.R. 368, at p. 374; Niles v. Lake, [1947] S.C.R. 291; Rathwell v. Rathwell, [1978] 2 S.C.R. 436, at p. 451; J. Sopinka, S. N. Lederman and A. W. Bryant, The Law of Evidence in Canada (2nd ed. 1999), at p. 115.
authorities.authority: The presumption of resulting trust and advancement are rebuttable presumptions of law as established in cases such as Re Mailman Estate, Niles v. Lake, Rathwell v. Rathwell, and discussed in The Law of Evidence in Canada.

authorities.quote: In addition, as noted by Feldman J.A. in the Ontario Court of Appeal in Saylor v. Madsen Estate (2005), 261 D.L.R. (4th) 597, the advantage of maintaining the presumption of advancement and the presumption of a resulting trust is that they provide a measure of certainty and predictability for individuals who put property in joint accounts or make other gratuitous transfers.
authorities.authority: The advantage of maintaining the presumption of advancement and the presumption of a resulting trust is that they provide a measure of certainty and predictability for individuals who put property in joint accounts or make other gratuitous transfers, as noted by Feldman J.A. in Saylor v. Madsen Estate.

authorities.quote: 29 One of the earliest documented cases where a judge applied the presumption of advancement is the 17th century decision in Grey (Lord) v. Grey (Lady) (1677), Rep. Temp. Finch 338, 23 E.R. 185: . . . the Law will never imply a Trust, because the natural Consideration of Blood, and the Obligation which lies on the Father in Conscience to provide for his Son, are predominant, and must over‑rule all manner of Implications.
authorities.authority: The 17th century case Grey v. Grey established that a father has an obligation to provide for his son, justifying the presumption of advancement.

authorities.quote: This has also been the conclusion of the weight of judicial opinion in recent times: see e.g. Mordo v. Nitting, [2006] B.C.J. No. 3081 (QL), 2006 BCSC 1761, at paras. 233-38; Shaw v. MacKenzie Estate (1994), 4 E.T.R. (2d) 306 (N.S.S.C.), at para. 49; and Reber v. Reber (1988), 48 D.L.R. (4th) 376 (B.C.S.C.); see also Waters’ Law of Trusts, at p. 406.
authorities.authority: Recent judicial opinion supports that survivorship rights vest inter vivos when the joint account is opened.

authorities.quote: 49 An early case that addressed the issue of the nature of survivorship is Re Reid in which Ferguson J.A. of the Ontario Court of Appeal found that the gift of a joint interest was a “complete and perfect gift inter vivos” (p. 608) from the moment that the joint account was opened even though the transferor in that case retained exclusive control over the account during his lifetime.
authorities.authority: Re Reid held that the gift of a joint interest is a complete and perfect inter vivos gift from the moment the joint account is opened, even if transferor retains exclusive control during lifetime.

authorities.quote: I also find MacKay J.A.’s reasons in Edwards v. Bradley (C.A.), at p. 234, to be persuasive: The legal right to take the balance in the account if A predeceases him being vested in B on the opening of the account, it cannot be the subject of a testamentary disposition. If A’s intention was that B should also have the beneficial interest, B already has the legal title and there is nothing further to be done to complete the gift of the beneficial interest. If A’s intention was that B should not take the beneficial interest, it belongs to A or his estate and he is not attempting to dispose of it by means of the joint account. In either event B has the legal title and the only question that can arise on A’s death is whether B is entitled to keep any money that may be in the account on A’s death or whether he holds it as a trustee under a resulting trust for A’s estate. [Emphasis added.] Edwards v. Bradley was appealed to the Supreme Court of Canada but the issue of survivorship was not addressed.
authorities.authority: MacKay J.A.'s reasons in Edwards v. Bradley are persuasive that the legal right to the balance vests on opening the account and cannot be testamentary.

authorities.quote: 51 Treating survivorship in these circumstances as an inter vivos gift of a joint interest has found favour in other jurisdictions, including Australia and the United Kingdom: see Russell v. Scott (1936), 55 C.L.R. 440, at p. 455; Young v. Sealey, [1949] 1 All E.R. 92 (Ch. Div.), at pp. 107-8; (in obiter) Aroso v. Coutts, [2002] 1 All E.R. (Comm) 241, [2001] EWHC Ch 443, at paras. 29 and 36.
authorities.authority: Other jurisdictions like Australia and the UK favour treating survivorship as an inter vivos gift of a joint interest.

authorities.quote: 52 While not entirely analogous, the American notion of the “Totten trust” (sometimes referred to as the “Bank account trust”) is now recognized as valid in most states in the United States; an individual places money in a bank account with the instruction that upon his or her death, whatever is in that bank account will pass to a named beneficiary: see Restatement (Third) of Trusts (2003), at para. 26 of Part 2, Chapter 5. The Totten trust is so named for the leading case establishing its validity: see Matter of Totten, 179 N.Y. 112 (1904). While a Totten trust does not deal with joint accounts as such, it recognizes the practicality of the depositor having control of an account during his or her lifetime but allowing the depositor’s named beneficiary of that account to claim the funds remaining in the account upon the death of the depositor without the disposition being treated as testamentary: see e.g. Matter of Berson, 566 N.Y.S.2d 74 (App. Div. 1991); Matter of Halpern, 303 N.Y. 33 (1951).
authorities.authority: The American Totten trust recognizes the depositor's control during lifetime and the beneficiary's right to remaining funds at death without the disposition being testamentary.

authorities.quote: As noted by Huband J.A. in Dreger, at para. 33: “Self-serving statements after the event are too easily fabricated in order to bring about a desired result.”
authorities.authority: Huband J.A. in Dreger noted that self-serving statements after the event are easily fabricated to achieve a desired result.

authorities.quote: In Lavelle v. Lavelle, [2004] EWCA Civ 223 (BAILII), at para. 19, Lord Phillips, M.R., had this to say about Shephard v. Cartwright and certain other authorities relied on by the appellant in that case: It seems to me that it is not satisfactory to apply rigid rules of law to the evidence that is admissible to rebut the presumption of advancement. Plainly, self-serving statements or conduct of a transferor, who may long after the transaction be regretting earlier generosity, carry little or no weight.
authorities.authority: In Lavelle v. Lavelle, Lord Phillips stated that rigid rules on admissible evidence to rebut presumption of advancement are unsatisfactory and self-serving statements long after the transaction carry little weight.

authorities.quote: 83 Similarly, in Nelson v. Nelson (1995), 184 C.L.R. 538, the High Court of Australia dealt with a case involving a mother’s purchase of a house which she then transferred into the names of her children. In his concurring reasons, McHugh J. made the following comments about the presumption of resulting trust: No doubt in earlier centuries, the practices and modes of thought of the property owning classes made it more probable than not that, when a person transferred property in such circumstances, the transferor did not intend the transferee to have the beneficial as well as the legal interest in the property. But times change. To my mind — and, I think, to the minds of most people — it seems much more likely that, in the absence of an express declaration or special circumstances, the transfer of property without consideration was intended as a gift to the transferee. . . . A presumption is a useful aid to decision making only when it accurately reflects the probability that a fact or state of affairs exists or has occurred. . . . If the presumptions do not reflect common experience today, they may defeat the expectations of those who are unaware of them.
authorities.authority: The High Court of Australia in Nelson v. Nelson recognized that times have changed and it is more likely that a gratuitous transfer was intended as a gift unless there is express declaration or special circumstances; presumptions should reflect common experience to avoid defeating expectations.

authorities.quote: 92 Even at the elemental stage in the development of the doctrine, the court in Grey (Lord) v. Grey (Lady) (1677), 2 Swans. 594, 36 E.R. 742, identified natural affection as a rationale for the application of the presumption of advancement: For the natural consideration of blood and affection is so apparently predominant, that those acts which would imply a trust in a stranger, will not do so in a son; and, ergo, the father who would check and control the appearance of nature, ought to provide for himself by some instrument, or some clear proof of a declaration of trust, and not depend upon any implication of law . . . . [Emphasis added; p. 743.]
authorities.authority: The court in Grey (Lord) v. Grey (Lady) identified natural affection as a rationale for the presumption of advancement, requiring clear proof of trust to rebut it.

left_open.quote: I can say no more than these are matters for determination between the Canada Revenue Agency and taxpayers in specific cases.
left_open.issue: The Court will not decide tax matters between the Canada Revenue Agency and taxpayers in specific cases.
